lead: Check a phone backup or dump for signs of known spyware. MVT, the Mobile Verification Toolkit, was released by Amnesty International's Security Lab in 2021 and works on both iOS and Android data.
use_when: You have an iOS backup or an Android backup or bug report and want to compare it with published spyware indicators.
The device owner has agreed to the analysis. The project says MVT is for consensual analysis only.
You want records such as messages, calls, browser history and installed apps pulled out as JSON files.

features.title: Three command line tools
items: mvt-ios for iPhone and iPad data
mvt for shared tasks such as downloading indicators

features.title: iOS checks
items: Reads an iTunes or Finder backup, and can decrypt an encrypted backup with the password
Can also check a file system dump and a sysdiagnose archive
Extracts records such as SMS, calls, contacts, Safari and Chrome history, WhatsApp data and installed applications

features.title: Android checks
items: Checks a standalone Android bug report
Checks the SMS messages in an Android backup made with adb backup

features.title: Indicators of compromise
items: Compares extracted records with indicators in STIX2 files
Can download public indicator lists with one command
Matches are shown in the terminal and saved to JSON files with a detected suffix in the name

formats: Android backup (.ab file or unpacked folder, SMS only)
requirements: You need Python 3.11 or newer. On Linux install a few system packages such as sqlite3 and libusb. On macOS the project asks for Xcode and Homebrew. The project does not officially support running natively on Windows and recommends WSL. The project says you should understand forensic basics and the command line to use it.

steps.title: Install it
steps.text: The project recommends installing with pipx. Install pipx first from your package manager, then run the command below. If the commands are not found afterwards, run pipx ensurepath and open a new terminal. On Windows, use WSL.

steps.title: Download the public indicators
steps.text: This fetches indicator lists from the project's indicators repository and stores them where MVT loads them automatically. You can also pass your own STIX2 file later with --iocs.

steps.title: Get the data to check
steps.text: For iOS, make a backup with iTunes or Finder, or with pymobiledevice3. For Android, collect data with AndroidQF, take a bug report, or make an SMS backup with adb backup. Get the owner's consent first. Work on a copy.

steps.title: Decrypt an encrypted iOS backup
steps.text: Skip this if the backup is not encrypted. The destination folder will hold the decrypted copy. MVT asks for the password if you leave out -p.

steps.title: Run the check
steps.text: Point the command at the backup folder and give an output folder for the JSON results. Without --output nothing is saved to disk.

steps.title: Check an Android source
steps.text: Use the command that matches how you collected the data. This example is for an AndroidQF folder. For a bug report use check-bugreport. For an SMS backup use check-backup.

steps.title: Read the results
steps.text: Open the JSON files in the output folder. Files with a detected suffix hold indicator matches. A match needs human review. No match does not prove the phone is clean.

cases.title: Suspected targeted spyware
cases.why: It compares phone records with indicators published for known campaigns, such as those from Amnesty International.

cases.title: Suspected stalkerware
cases.why: The project lists a public stalkerware indicator source that can be used with the same commands.

cases.title: Reviewing messages for malicious links
cases.why: URLs found in messages are extracted and, when you set an output folder, written to a file for review.

cases.title: Support for journalists and activists
cases.why: The project points civil society users to expert help from Amnesty International's Security Lab and Access Now's Digital Security Helpline.

cases.title: Study of mobile forensics methods
cases.why: The documentation explains the trade-offs between backups, file system dumps and sysdiagnose, which is useful teaching material.

strengths: Free and open source, built by a human rights organisation's security lab.
One tool covers both iOS and Android.
Uses the open STIX2 format, so you can add indicators from several sources.
Clear documentation site with a page for each acquisition method.
limits: It is a triage and detection tool. It is not a general phone forensics suite and it does not do full app parsing.
Public indicators cannot show that a device is clean. The project says relying on them alone can give a false sense of security.
The license prohibits using it on devices of people who have not consented. It is not for adversarial forensics.
Direct Android analysis over adb has been removed. You must collect data with AndroidQF, a bug report or a backup first.
The Android backup check only covers SMS messages, and adb backup is deprecated.
An iOS file system dump needs a jailbreak, which can alter records. Not every device or iOS version can be jailbroken.
Windows is not officially supported. Use WSL.
